title: New: Your agent handles finances now
core_takeaway: Andrew Warner interviews Trent, creator of an open-source double-entry accounting package (spoken as 'Slowbooks') built so a CLI coding agent can read and write your books directly — the thing QuickBooks deliberately won't allow. The live demo drags a folder of trip receipts into a Claude Code session and files all six as categorized expenses with an audit log distinguishing AI-made from admin-made changes, then re-categorizes one by chat. The pitch is data sovereignty: no paywalls, native OS OCR so there are no dependencies, optional fully offline operation with a local Llama instance, and QuickBooks/Zoho import-export so trying it is risk-free.
key_points: The demo: drag a trip-receipts folder into the terminal, say 'file these as expenses', and the agent OCRs, categorizes and files all six receipts, returning a per-receipt breakdown and flagging anything ambiguous (an unreadable date, a pre-declared split bill) for verification.

Corrections happen in chat — 'make that office supplies instead of meals' — and every AI-originated change is recorded in the audit log as done by the system rather than by an admin, so it can be identified and backed out.

Andrew's on-record accusation: QuickBooks markets itself as AI-friendly and is championed at every new Claude connector launch, but in practice locks you to its own AI. He asked Claude directly what it cannot do — limited to profit-and-loss and cash-flow reports only (no balance sheet, no AR/AP aging), no inventory, no expense entry, no bills, no vendor management, no bill payments.

The software is a real double-entry journal with built-in AI analytics driven by your own API keys (e.g. drill-downs on who owes what and who is 30 days past due), but the creator explicitly recommends working from the CLI rather than the UI.
Bank connectivity runs through SimpleFIN at about $1.50/month for more accounts than most people have — contrasted with QuickBooks-style API access sitting behind $200-300/month paywalls.

No paywalls, free forever once downloaded, with a nonprofit mode for donations and projections; the creator argues no cloud accounting company could match this without abandoning its business model, and frames community-built software as the future for personal and small-business tools.

OCR uses the native Windows OCR tool on Windows and the native macOS OCR tool on Mac, so there are zero extra installs; the OCR review UI lets you highlight a region and correct which field it is ('no, that's the merchant name'). The OCR failed live on camera on one file type, which the creator attributed to the demo file rather than the software.
Interoperability both ways: import and export IIF and other formats from QuickBooks, Zoho ('Soho') and GnuCash, so migrating in and back out is low-risk.

The project itself was built with Claude Code, Codex and Grok CLI, has over a dozen contributors, and showed 344 GitHub stars live on air; Andrew's call to action is to star it purely as a message to the financial-software industry about agent access to your own data.
why_it_matters: This is the clearest worked example of the pattern an AI tooling suite should study: incumbent SaaS gates its API precisely where agents would be most useful, so the winning move is an open, local, CLI-addressable data store the agent can drive directly. The design choices are the transferable part — native OS OCR to avoid dependencies, an audit log that distinguishes AI writes from human writes, bring-your-own API keys, and full offline operation with a local model. The audit-log-by-actor pattern in particular is a reusable primitive for any tool that lets an agent mutate real records.
